issues.title: Broad Environmental Representation Exposes City to Liability
issues.description: In Section 6.D , the City makes an extraordinarily broad representation that the Premises "has never, and does not currently contain, nor is it contaminated by, any hazardous or toxic waste materials." This is extremely risky given that the attached Phase II ESA (Exhibit B) itself documents the presence of petroleum hydrocarbons, PCBs, lead, benzene, toluene, and asbestos-containing materials on the site — a former steel manufacturing complex appearing on EPA's RCRA/CERCLA list . The qualifier "in violation of any applicable environmental laws" provides some protection, but the sweeping "has never" language is overbroad and factually questionable for a former industrial site. The City should narrow this representation to be limited to its actual knowledge and the ESA findings.

issues.comment: We qualified this representation to reflect the City's actual knowledge as informed by the attached Phase II ESA, which is the appropriate standard for a former industrial site appearing on EPA's RCRA/CERCLA list; an unqualified historical warranty of no contamination is neither commercially standard nor factually supportable here.

judgment.reason: The issue concerns the factual breadth and commercial risk of an unqualified warranty, not an ambiguity or internal contradiction. The express exception for matters in Exhibit B substantially reconciles the representation with the ESA findings.

issues.title: Absolute Lien-Free and No-Litigation Warranties Too Broad
issues.description: In Section 6.B , the City makes an absolute warranty that the Premises "shall be clear of all liens and claims of any party" and that "there are no claims, actions, suits, or proceedings instituted, filed or threatened, which may affect the Premises" . For a former LTV Steel industrial site that was acquired via quit claim deed and appears on EPA's RCRA/CERCLA list, these absolute representations carry significant risk. The City should qualify these warranties with a knowledge qualifier and limit the lien representation to liens created by or through the City.

Given the environmental sensitivity of the site and Hardrives' intended industrial use, the indemnification should be broadened to include environmental liability, property damage, and regulatory fines.

issues.title: License is Revocable by Nature — No Protection Against Early Termination
issues.description: This agreement grants a "license" rather than a lease. Under Ohio law, a license is generally revocable at will by the licensor. The agreement does not expressly state that the license is irrevocable during its term, which creates risk for Hardrives — particularly given that Hardrives intends to invest in using the Premises for production operations and corporate offices . Hardrives should seek language making the license irrevocable during the term, or alternatively, the agreement should be restructured as a lease to provide greater possessory rights.

judgments.title: Broad Environmental Representation Exposes City to Liability
judgments.reason: The issue concerns the factual breadth and commercial risk of an unqualified warranty, not an ambiguity or internal contradiction. The express exception for matters in Exhibit B substantially reconciles the representation with the ESA findings.

judgments.title: "As Is" Acceptance Should Disclaim Additional Warranties
judgments.reason: The issue seeks broader warranty disclaimers rather than identifying ambiguity. Section 8 expressly preserves the City’s stated representations, so the as-is language is reconcilable with them.

judgments.title: City's Environmental Warranty Lacks Indemnification for Pre-Existing Contamination
judgments.reason: The absence of a City indemnity for pre-existing contamination is a risk-allocation omission, not an ambiguity or conflict among existing provisions.

judgments.title: No Right of Inspection Reserved for City
judgments.reason: The absence of a contractual inspection right is a substantive omission and negotiation concern, not an ambiguity or inconsistency in existing text.

judgments.title: Insurance Amount May Be Inadequate for Former Industrial Site
judgments.reason: Whether $1 million is adequate insurance is a commercial risk-allocation question; the stated amount is textually definite.

judgments.title: Insurance Coverage Lacks Specificity
judgments.reason: The phrase “in the amount of $1,000,000.00” does not specify whether the insurance limit applies per occurrence or in the aggregate, creating a genuine scope ambiguity.

judgments.title: Environmental Compliance Obligation Potentially Overbroad
judgments.reason: The undefined phrase “any hazardous material or waste” has uncertain boundaries and may or may not encompass ordinary asphalt, petroleum products, solvents, and similar operational materials.

judgments.title: No Right to Remove Improvements or Personal Property on Termination
judgments.reason: The requirement to “surrender the Premises … in as good a condition as received” does not clearly establish whether Hardrives may or must remove later-added trade fixtures, equipment, or improvements.

judgments.title: Indemnification Scope Should Cover Environmental Claims
judgments.reason: The term “injury” may mean bodily injury alone or legal injury more broadly, including property or environmental harm. That lexical uncertainty affects the indemnity’s scope.

judgments.title: Environmental Compliance Limited to "EPA" Laws Only
judgments.reason: “Environmental Protection Agency laws or regulations” is uncertain as to whether it means only federal EPA-administered requirements, Ohio EPA requirements, or both.

judgments.title: Overly Broad Indemnification by Hardrives
judgments.reason: The causal phrases “resulting from injury on or about the Premises” and “in conjunction with” Hardrives’ use are broad enough to leave uncertain whether the indemnity includes the City’s negligence, third-party conduct, or pre-existing conditions.

judgments.title: License Grant Lacks Revocability Language
judgments.reason: The grant of a “license for use” does not state whether it is revocable at will or protected for the stated term. Its revocability could therefore require construction in light of the agreement’s fixed-term language.

judgments.title: License is Revocable by Nature — No Protection Against Early Termination
judgments.reason: The grant of a “license” without express revocability language leaves room to dispute whether it is revocable at will or irrevocable during the stated term, especially given the contemplated operational investment.

judgments.title: No Notice Provision in Agreement
judgments.reason: “Upon written notice by the City” does not establish an authorized delivery method or whether notice is effective upon sending or receipt, leaving the cure period’s trigger uncertain.

judgments.title: Conflict Between Non-Assignment and Successors/Assigns Provision
judgments.reason: Section 12’s inclusion of “assigns” is in tension with Section 9’s prohibition on assignment without consent, even though a court could harmonize them by reading “assigns” as permitted assigns.

judgments.title: Survival Clause Is Overbroad
judgments.reason: “Shall survive” does not specify the endpoint or duration of survival, leaving uncertainty over whether the obligations continue through termination indefinitely or only for a reasonable period.

judgments.title: Contradiction Between Non-Assignment and Successors/Assigns Binding
judgments.reason: Section 12’s reference to “assigns” is in tension with Section 9’s consent requirement for assignment, although the provisions may be harmonized by limiting Section 12 to permitted assigns.

judgments.title: Premises Definition Overly Broad with "Including But Not Limited To"
judgments.reason: “Including, but not limited to” places an unrestricted catch-all against the specifically described Parcel No. 3, making the geographic scope of the Premises uncertain.

judgments.title: Exhibit A Description Broader Than Parcel No. 3
judgments.reason: The general phrase “including, but not limited to” sits against the specific legal description of Parcel No. 3 and makes the licensed property’s outer boundaries uncertain.

judgments.title: City Warrants Surplus Declaration Before It May Have Occurred
judgments.reason: “Will be declared” leaves unclear when the surplus declaration must occur and whether it is a condition precedent to the license or merely a future covenant.

judgments.title: Surplus Property Declaration May Create Risk
judgments.reason: The future-tense phrase “will be declared” leaves uncertain whether the surplus declaration is a condition precedent, a future covenant, or an event expected outside the agreement.

judgments.title: No Payment Due Date Specified for Annual Rental
judgments.reason: Section 4 depends on “the date payment is due,” while Section 3 establishes no due date. Reading the payment and default provisions together leaves the default trigger operationally indeterminate.

judgments.title: No City Right to Terminate for Cause Beyond Payment Default
judgments.reason: By expressly identifying nonpayment as an “event of default” while omitting all other breaches, Section 4 raises an expressio unius question about whether other breaches can trigger termination.

judgments.title: Typo in number
judgments.reason: “Thirty (80) days” contains inconsistent written and numerical values, a mechanical error that changes the applicable deadline.

judgments.title: Cure Period Too Short for Default
judgments.reason: The ten-day cure period is definite; whether it is too short or disproportionate is a negotiation and equitable-remedy concern rather than a construction defect.

judgments.title: No Notice Provision
judgments.reason: The phrase “written notice” omits the required delivery method and effective time, leaving uncertainty about when the ten-day cure period begins.

judgments.title: No Payment Due Date Specified
judgments.reason: Section 4 invokes a payment due date that Section 3 never supplies, so the annual rental and default provisions cannot together yield a definite default date.

judgments.title: Typo in number
judgments.reason: The mismatch between “thirty” and “(80)” is a numerical drafting error that creates two different deadlines.

judgments.title: No Holdover or Post-Expiration Provisions
judgments.reason: The word “or” between the one-year term and the title-conveyance endpoint does not clearly establish which endpoint controls, particularly if conveyance never occurs.

judgments.title: Undefined term: Development Agreement
judgments.reason: “Development Agreement” is not defined or otherwise identified beyond a general description of a future agreement, leaving uncertainty about the instrument that triggers title transfer.

judgments.title: Default Provision Only Addresses Payment — No City Default
judgments.reason: The absence of an express City-default provision is a substantive remedial omission; it does not itself make the existing payment-default or term provisions ambiguous or contradictory.

judgments.title: Undefined term: Development Agreement
judgments.reason: The undefined capitalized term “Development Agreement” does not identify the precise future instrument whose execution and performance relate to conveyance and the license term.

judgments.title: No Automatic Renewal or Extension Provision
judgments.reason: Section 5’s alternative term endpoints do not clearly state what happens if the Development Agreement or conveyance never occurs, making the duration of the license uncertain.
